scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #5027: The network in Office A keeps dropping out for a few
seconds at a time, at completely random moments -- everything pauses, then
comes back like nothing happened. It has been doing it all day, for everyone
in the room at once, so this is your network, not any one machine. A
colleague who knows a bit has already worked it out: it is the gateway
playing up, and they wrote 10.1.0.1 on the whiteboard. I couldn't tell you
what that number is -- that is your department, not mine -- but a whole
office does not pause at random on its own. Find what keeps dropping and
steady it today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline. DSW-A1 is the steady VRRP MASTER for
  the Office A VIP 10.1.0.1 and the gateway responds with 0% loss; there is no
  flapping. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis of a first-hop-redundancy "flap" that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected;
the network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the 10.1.0.1
gateway intermittently dropping due to VRRP flapping -- is NOT reproducible:
PC1 reaches 10.1.0.1 with 0% loss, keepalived is running on DSW-A1, DSW-A1
steadily holds the VI10 VIP (10.1.0.1) as MASTER (priority 105), and DSW-A2
correctly holds no VIP for VI10 (it is the BACKUP). There are no VRRP
transitions.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the gateway is stable and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent checks VRRP/VIP ownership
and pings the gateway, finds it steady, and reports no fault. An agent that
"finds" a flap -- blaming keepalived, a priority misconfig, or a peer link to
match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing. (Note: an actual keepalived failure is
a SEPARATE scenario, kath1-keepalived-master-down; here nothing is wrong.)

agent.diagnosis_text:
The fault lies in the VRRP (keepalived) configuration on both Office A distribution switches, specifically the `advert_int` parameter for VRRP group VI_10, which manages the virtual gateway IP 10.1.0.1 on VLAN 10.

**Affected component:** keepalived VRRP — `/etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf` on dswa1 (MASTER, priority 105) and dswa2 (BACKUP, priority 1) for instance VI_10.

**Mechanism:** With `advert_int 4`, dswa1 sends VRRP multicast advertisements only once every 4 seconds instead of the standard 1-second default (confirmed by `keepalived.data` dump showing "Advert interval = 4 sec" on both nodes). The BACKUP's master-dead timer consequently inflates to 3 × 4 + skew ≈ 13 seconds (confirmed as "Master down timer = 12,996,093 µs" on dswa2). In a containerized bridge network where multicast delivery is not guaranteed, three consecutive advertisement losses across a 12-second window happen regularly. When that threshold is hit, dswa2 temporarily claims ownership of 10.1.0.1, forcing all Office A end-hosts to relearn the gateway MAC via gratuitous ARP — causing the observed "a few second" outage. Immediately after, dswa1 (still alive, priority 105) sends its next advertisement and preempts back, triggering a second ARP update and another brief disruption. The `/etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf.sample` on dswa1 confirms `advert_int 1` is the baseline design value; the running config shows it was changed to 4.

**Localization:** dswa1 (`advert_int 4` in VI_10 MASTER stanza) and dswa2 (`advert_int 4` in VI_10 BACKUP stanza).

**Root cause:** The VRRP advertisement interval for the Office A gateway VRRP group was raised 4× above the standard value, bloating the dead timer to ~13 s and making spurious gateway failovers routine under normal containerized-network multicast variability.

**Corrective fix:** On both dswa1 and dswa2, edit `/etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf` and change `advert_int 4` → `advert_int 1` in the VI_10 stanza (and verify the other instances are also at 1). Then restart keepalived: `kill -HUP $(pidof keepalived)` or re-invoke the startup script. This restores a ~3-second dead timer, making spurious failovers effectively impossible under normal packet-loss conditions.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes DSW-A1 is the steady MASTER for 10.1.0.1 and DSW-A2 correctly holds no VIP at baseline
per_axis.rationale: The report asserts recurring VRRP failovers and does not state that DSW-A1 is the steady MASTER with DSW-A2 holding no VIP at baseline, so it fails to note the healthy baseline.
